summary: Seven screenshots and the surrounding Telegram thread establish waves, bucket dispatch, dependency gates, halt attribution, Doctor/Warden controls, prompt version chains, and a safe-change workflow. Canonical storage, complete state machines, workspace isolation, merge/replan details, auto-heal allowlist, end-to-end lineage, and quality proof remain unknown.
facts: A wave contains multiple typed subtasks and is distinct from the execution bucket.
Dependency readiness blocks normal dispatch but a human override is visible.
Halt attribution uses declared write_set and actual dirty/diff paths with exact/partial/none confidence.
Prompt versions carry role/layer/version/commit/parent/champion metadata, but the shown versions say eval not measured.
No evidence identifies the canonical storage engine or complete transition tables.
The first-pass/no-bugs claim lacks a baseline, denominator, observation window, and escaped-defect data.
contradictions: Nikolay says dangerous Git resets are prohibited, while the UI command log shows controlled git restore/clean operations; this is compatible only if the policy distinguishes user/agent commands from trusted recovery actions.

The system is described as producing controlled quality, while the shown prompt version chain has no measured eval; controlled quality may rely on other tests/gates, but prompt-quality attribution is not yet demonstrated.
ambiguity_requiring_judge: Choose the canonical change/event store and projection boundary.
Choose wave/task/attempt schemas and transition ownership.
Choose worktree/branch isolation and merge/replan strategy.
Choose halt taxonomy and auto-heal allowlist.
Choose immutable lineage identifiers and quality metrics.
Choose how many launch queues can be safely defined before implementation feedback.
